data_section_spans.heading: 3.1 Sample selection
data_section_spans.start_anchor: Our sample consists of private lending agreements

data_section_full_text:
Our sample consists of private lending agreements drawn from the 2007 release of
Dealscan and covers the period 1992–2007. We use the automated search features in
Dealscan to obtain a sample of 3,082 loans with current ratio covenants. As
indicated in Dichev and Skinner (2002), the current ratio is uniformly defined in
debt covenants. Consequently, measurement error related to the closeness to
violation of the current ratio covenant is reduced. <sup>3</sup> We obtain the requisite financial
data from the Compustat database. We could not obtain financial data for 1,237
loans because either COMPUSTAT or Dealscan did not include the ticker symbols.
We could manually match 725 of these 1,237 loans to COMPUSTAT and included
them in our final sample. These sample selection procedures resulted in a final
sample of 2,195 loans covering 1,009 firms and 14,816 loan quarters.

We adjust the current ratio sample for any current ratio covenants that vary over
the life of the loan. Because our interest is in testing the effect of covenants on
earnings management, we attempt to identify the effective life for each loan, i.e., the
time during which the loan is actually binding and therefore most likely to affect
earnings management behavior. Dealscan includes only the projected loan life,
which may differ from the effective life. We estimate the effective life of each loan
using the procedures described in Dichev and Skinner (2002) for any loans
refinanced, rolled over, amended, or replaced before the projected maturity date. <sup>4</sup>

Dichev and Skinner (2002) perform all their tests on both their full sample of active
and inactive loans and their subsample of active deals only. Their findings indicate
that there are no significant differences across these two loan samples. Therefore we
conduct our tests on the full sample that includes both active loans and inactive
loans for which we estimate the effective life. <sup>5</sup>

We divide our sample of loans with current ratio covenants into three
subsamples: (1) loans that are far from violation of their debt covenants (FAR),
(2) loans that are close to but not in violation of their debt covenants (CLOSE), and
(3) loans that are currently in violation of their debt covenants (DEFAULT). We


3 In a robustness test, we also consider net worth covenants.

4 Dealscan includes the average life for most loans. Using the average life to represent the effective life
of the loan does not change the main conclusions.

5 We also conduct our analysis on the active sample only. The results (not tabulated) are qualitatively
similar.

Impact of proximity to debt covenant violation 481


classify a loan as FAR, CLOSE, or DEFAULT based on the proximity to its current
ratio covenant. We measure covenant proximity as the difference between the actual
value of the covenant variable at the end of the quarter and the stated value of the
covenant in the debt agreement divided by the stated value of the covenant. We
classify loans with greater than 15 % covenant proximity as FAR, loans with
covenant proximity between zero and 15 % as CLOSE, and loans with negative
covenant proximity as DEFAULT. <sup>6</sup> Following this procedure, 54.8 % of the loans
are classified as FAR, 24.9 % as CLOSE, and 20.3 % as DEFAULT.
